title: Lying Power Versus Lasting Love
overview: The writer confronts a powerful man who ruins others with lies, says God will bring him down, and contrasts him with someone who trusts God's steady love.

parts.label: Calling out the boaster (v. 1)
parts.note: The heading links this psalm to Doeg, an official of King Saul who reported a priest for helping the fleeing David and then carried out Saul's order to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22). The second line is hard to read in Hebrew, so some translations make it a reminder that God's love lasts, while others call the boaster a disgrace to God.

parts.label: A tongue like a razor (vv. 2-4)
parts.note: The charge is about words: lies and twisted reports that cut quietly but deeply, like a sharp razor. In the background story his report was partly true but left out what would have cleared the priest, and his words were aimed at destroying people.

parts.label: Uprooted like a plant (v. 5)
parts.note: God will do to him what he did to others, pulling him from his tent and tearing him out of the land of the living like a plant by its roots. Some read 'tent' as God's sacred tent, meaning he also loses his place in worship.

parts.label: The onlookers' verdict (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Good people react with awe and even laughter at his fall, which can sound harsh to modern ears. Their point is that he leaned on his wealth and grew strong by harming others instead of relying on God.

parts.label: An olive tree in God's house (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: By contrast, the writer pictures himself as an olive tree, known for long life and fruit, growing in God's house and rooted in God's lasting love. He promises to thank God openly among the faithful and to keep hoping in God's 'name', meaning God's character as shown in what God has done.

think: What do people tend to lean on to feel secure, and what happens to them when it gives way?
